Senses.Explanation: Fix the mind and contemplate stillness names holding the mind in place while taking quiet as what is to be observed. The Platform record puts the wording in Zhicheng's report of Shenxiu's instruction; Huineng immediately calls it an illness rather than Zen and questions the value of prolonged sitting. Wanfeng Shiwei groups it with raising the mind to look outward, gathering the mind to clarify inwardly, and congealing the mind to enter the Way. Songyuan Chongyue quotes Linji Yixuan condemning the same four-part list. Tianran Hanshi likewise questions the difference between prolonged sitting and taking this as final. These sources record the procedure through criticism; they do not present it here as Zen instruction.
Senses.Note: The sources preserve the wording as a procedure they question or explicitly reject; the entry does not endorse it.

Senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, the rank “absolute within the relative” (偏中正) names the absolute or upright disclosed within the relative or differentiated, reversing the nesting of “relative within the absolute” while remaining paired with it in explanations and verse sequences. Caoshan Benji glosses the rank as leaving affairs and entering principle. The Eyes of Humans and Devas transmits the same affairs-to-principle gloss in its Five Ranks account. Hongzhi Zhengjue gives the rank a sea-cloud, sacred-peak, returning-traveler, and mirror image. Langting Ting pairs it with a yellow bird carrying spring news. Juelang Daosheng associates it with a western circle and lesser yin, while Ruibai Mingxue identifies the same shout as this rank when it is silent right where it occurs. Tianran Hanshi reports Dongshan's old-woman-and-mirror stanza and answers it with another mirror verse; the varied images illustrate rather than define the relation.

Senses.Explanation: The side position is the differentiated member of Caodong positional language: it is where forms, speech, and responsive activity are located in contrast with the straight position. Caoshan Benji identifies it with the realm in which myriad forms appear, then turns that classification into an interview test when an unnamed monastic interlocutor claims to come from the side position. Linquan Conglun preserves the refusal in his appraisal. Yongjue Yuanxian classifies merit and royal-son sequences as matters on this side while warning against mechanically mapping separate schemes together. Baiyu and Dahui Zonggao both expose a limit: diagrams and verbal explanations can themselves remain side-position talk. The term therefore names a relational position inside these attested schemes; it is not a general synonym for error, inferiority, or one physical side.

Senses.Note: The pair can name Caodong positions, but the records also use it more broadly for a distinction that speech or perception may make, miss, or coordinate.

Senses.Explanation: The question is already at work in the answer, and the answer begins from the point exposed by the question: in this Zen interview formula, the two turns meet rather than operate as a request followed by detachable information. Yuanwu Keqin quotes the line from an unnamed ancient voice while explaining Yunmen Wenyan's three-character reply, 'one answering statement.' He calls the exchange sharply solitary and asks where that sharpness lies; Yuanwu describes Yunmen's questioner as an adept and the answer as meeting that exact point like a heavy iron hammer driving a wedge. It does not claim that every question contains its verbal solution, and the exact final-word form remains a one-work provisional entry.

Senses.Explanation: A question-and-answer exchange is the asking-and-answering unit preserved in Chan encounters and records. In Zhaozhou's record, an unnamed monk asks how the master answers if every question-and-answer falls within the thinking faculty; Zhaozhou replies, “Ask.” The expression also labels documentary form: Zhongfeng Mingben's record notes that a question-and-answer was not recorded, and the Record of the Mirror of the School assigns a question-and-answer division the job of removing doubt. The format alone does not establish a successful Chan encounter. Foyan Qingyuan criticizes people who simply take question-and-answer to be the Chan house style. Juyun Chuiwan Guangzhen says that a genuine question requires an apt answer and calls a mismatched pair deaf and blind to one another; Yingshan Zhiyin likewise conditions fluent question-and-answer on correctly assessing the exchanges already raised.

問處 is the place or point at which a question bears. Yuanwu rejects the claim that the question itself settles the matter; the Ancient Worthies record uses the phrase for the point at which a teacher seizes a student, and Tianjing Xin contrasts Mazu’s question-point with Nanyuan’s answer-point. The records use the term for a determinate place within an exchange, not for a separate object or doctrine.

Senses.Explanation: Pinching the eyes to produce flowers names an illusion manufactured by forcing or distorting one's own sight. Pinjixiang Zhixiang and Yingning Zhijing apply it while criticizing inherited displays around Shakyamuni and Mahakasyapa. Zhe'an Jingfan says cultivation and realization can amount to this eye-made display; Yushan Shangsi compares further explanatory speech to it; Foyan Qingyuan warns that seeing matters this way goes astray; and Mingjue Cong rejects taking such appearances as real form. Across these uses, the flowers are not a discovery but an artifact of the attempt to see.
